newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Q4 ECI eases fears of wage, inflation spike.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Q4 ECI eases fears of wage, inflation spike.

text.p: A surprisingly benevolent report on U.S. labor costs in the fourth quarter brought waves of relief to economists and investors and may help delay a widely anticipated Federal Reserve credit tightening, analysts said.

The Labor Department reported the Employment Cost Index rose 0.8 percent over the last three months on 1996, slightly less than the 0.9 percent consensus forecast of a Reuters poll, squashing fears of a dangerous inflation spike, economists said.

"The Federal Reserve is likely to remain on hold, not just at the February (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting, but through the first half of the year and perhaps a little bit longer," said Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch.

While the headline number came in only slightly better than expected, analysts said they had fretted over a potential surprise burst of wage gains, so they breathed a sigh of relief at the relatively modest figure.
"A lot of people thought there was upside risk. Things could have been worse," said Kenneth Mayland, chief economist at Society National Bank.
Wages and salaries rose 3.3 percent over the full year 1996, but more modest growth of 2.0 percent in benefits costs kept total compensation gains at 2.9 percent.
Those represent only slight increases from 1995 total compensation growth of 2.7 percent in 1995 and wages and salaries growth of 2.9 percent.
But analysts cautioned that any increase in compensation costs at this stage of the economic expansion could cause trouble.
"The issue is trend," said Mayland, noting the 1996 wage and salary gains were the largest since 1991.

After six years of uninterrupted economic growth and a jobless rate of 5.3 percent cofirming anecdotal evidence of tight labor markets, benign wage and inflation data may soon give way to ever increasing price pressures, analysts said.
"Worse numbers will probably be forthcoming in 1997," said Mayland. "This report provides momentary relief from the tight labor markets issue, but it doesn't take it off the table."
Yet wage growth alone might not prompt a major rise in overall inflation, analysts noted. For example, U.S. firms may tighten profit margins to keep prices down.
"Some pickup in costs this year is inevitable, but we expect any pickup to be slight," said Katz.
"Given the fact that competitive forces remain intense, any pickup in labor costs will probably erode profit margins rather than cause a pickup in the core (consumer price index," she added.

Investors immediately warmed to the ECI report, with the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond vaulting a full point higher and resting comfortably near its session highs an hour after the report's release.
"The number was benign and the markets are relieved," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities, Inc.
But that sentiment could easily worsen if ensuing data point towards price pressures building elsewhere, he added.

"Far more important are the dta we see next week in the (National Association of Purchasing Management Survey) and (January) payrolls," he said. "Where we're going is much more important than where we've been." (( --212-859-1664 ))
